claims.text: The proposed alloy is equiatomic Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti.
The alloy is produced by vacuum arc melting followed by homogenization at 1400–1600°C.
Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti will exhibit significantly reduced neutron activation.
Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti will retain excellent high-temperature strength.
Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti is a strong candidate for low-activation plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
Conventional refractory HEAs may contain higher-activation elements.
Traditional tungsten-based materials or plasma-facing ferritic/martensitic steels may not simultaneously satisfy low-activation and high-temperature performance requirements.
Ta, Nb, Hf, Zr, and Ti are intrinsically low-activation refractory elements relative to the elements they replace.
Homogenization at 1400–1600°C produces a homogeneous, single-phase microstructure in equiatomic Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti.
A homogeneous, single-phase microstructure minimizes phase inhomogeneities and brittleness.
The constituent refractory elements produce fewer long-lived radioactive isotopes upon neutron irradiation.
A stable, uniform microstructure preserves mechanical strength under extreme fusion-relevant conditions.
Relative to tungsten-based materials and ferritic/martensitic steels, Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti will generate fewer long-lived activation products.
Relative to tungsten-based materials and ferritic/martensitic steels, Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti will maintain comparable or improved high-temperature mechanical properties.
Relative to tungsten-based materials and ferritic/martensitic steels, Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti will maintain comparable or improved irradiation resistance.
The proposed benefits are expected to persist at operating temperatures up to approximately 1400–1600°C under typical fusion-reactor irradiation and thermal-flux conditions.
Small-scale processing variability may affect the uniformity of the desired microstructure.
